ybm_intro_consent@1.0/en-GB/self/standar.name: YBM introduction and consent

stem.text: MyPhone/MyBrain Intervention Study

lede.text:
Welcome back!

You are now completing the follow-up questionnaire for the My Phone My Brain study after your social media break.

We will ask you some questions about your wellbeing and digital behaviour so that we can compare your responses before and after the break. Your information will continue to be handled confidentially and stored securely in accordance with University of Leeds data-protection procedures.

Taking part remains voluntary. You can stop at any time or ask a member of the research team if anything is unclear.

This questionnaire should take approximately 10 minutes to complete. Please answer the questions carefully and as accurately as you can.

moreInfo.label: You can click below if you would like to review the full information about the study.

body.text:
What is the purpose of the study?
This study examines how short-term changes in smartphone use relate to brain activity, physiological responses, attention, and wellbeing. During laboratory sessions we will measure: Brain activity using electroencephalography (EEG), Heart activity using electrocardiography (ECG), and Eye movements using an eye-tracking system. To understand how changes in digital behaviour relate to these processes, the study also requires objective information about your smartphone and social media use.

Why have I been invited?
You have been invited because you are 18-24 years old and regularly use social media. The study aims to better understand how everyday digital behaviour relates to brain activity.

What will I be asked to do?
If you agree to participate, you will:
1.    Attend two laboratory sessions, approximately two hours each.
2.    Take a 30-day social media break using Brick to restrict agreed apps.
3.    Follow our guide to download, review, and clean your social media usage data, then upload it and your screen-time screenshots to Qualtrics.
4.    Complete brief weekly check-ins and share screen-time screenshots.

Laboratory Visits

Visit 1 – Baseline (~ 2 hours). During the first visit you will:
• Complete an EEG recording (measurement of brain activity)
• Complete an ECG recording (measurement of heart activity using small sensors on the skin)
• Use an eye-tracking system while completing computer tasks
• Perform computer-based cognitive tasks
• Complete questionnaires about wellbeing and digital behaviour

Visit 2 – Post-Intervention (~ 2 hours).) During the second visit you will:
• Repeat the EEG recording
• Repeat the ECG recording
• Complete eye-tracking during tasks
• Repeat the cognitive tasks
• Complete follow-up questionnaires

What is the social media abstinence period?
Between the two laboratory visits, you will be asked to take a 30-day break from social media.
A physical device called Brick will be used to restrict agreed social media apps on your smartphone. During this period, you will also be asked not to access the restricted platforms through internet browsers, laptops, tablets, other computers, or another person’s device or account. The platforms to be restricted will be agreed with you in advance.
WhatsApp may still be used for direct messages and calls. Essential phone functions, including calls, text messages, maps, banking, and email, will remain accessible.

If you decide you no longer wish to continue the restriction period, you may withdraw from the study at any time.

Smartphone and Social Media Usage Data 
As part of this study, you will be asked to share information about your smartphone and social media use. We will provide a step-by-step guide explaining how to download your TikTok and/or YouTube usage data and take screenshots of your phone’s Screen Time (Iphone) or Digital Wellbeing (Android) summary.
We will also provide a link to a data-cleaning tool that you can use to review and remove information from your downloaded data before uploading the cleaned files to Qualtrics. The guide will explain which usage information is needed for the study and how to prepare your files.

Sharing the required usage information is a necessary part of taking part in this study. If you have any questions or need help preparing your data, please contact the research team before uploading your files.

What is EEG?
EEG (electroencephalography) records natural electrical activity from the brain using small sensors placed on the scalp. EEG does not deliver electrical stimulation and is widely used in neuroscience research. You may feel mild pressure from the headset, but the procedure should not be painful.

What is ECG?
ECG (electrocardiography) measures the electrical activity of the heart using small sensors placed on the skin. The procedure is safe, painless, and commonly used in research and clinical settings.

What is eye-tracking?
Eye-tracking measures where and how your eyes move while you look at images or complete computer tasks. You will wear eye-tracking glasses that record your eye movements and where you look while completing computer tasks. The system does not record personal images or identify individuals.

Are there any risks?
There are no known serious risks associated with these measurements. Possible risks include: temporary inconvenience due to restricted access to selected smartphone applications and mild discomfort from wearing the EEG headset or ECG sensors

Do I have to take part?
No. Taking part is completely voluntary. You may withdraw from the study at any time without giving a reason and without any negative consequences.

Compensation
You will receive £25 for each completed laboratory visit, plus an additional £25 for completing all parts of the study, up to £75 in total. If you withdraw early, you will still receive £25 for each laboratory visit you have completed. There is no separate payment for each day of the social media break.

Confidentiality and Data Protection
The University of Leeds acts as the Data Controller for this research.
• Identifiable information will be stored separately from research data.
• Data will be labelled using a study ID code rather than your name.
• Results will be analysed and reported anonymously at the group level.
• Anonymised findings may be published in academic journals, conference presentations, reports, or academic theses.
You may request removal of your identifiable research data within one month after your final session. After this period, your data may have been anonymised, making it impossible to identify and remove your individual data..
The University Research Participant Privacy Notice is available at Privacy Notice for Research. This study has received ethical approval from the University of Leeds School of Psychology Research Ethics Committee [Ethics Reference: SoPrec 4202]

If you have any questions about this study, please contact:

Miftah Faizah

University of Leeds

lede.text:
Please tap each statement below to confirm that you understand and agree to it, and that you consent to take part in the study. We will move on once all statements are ticked.

As part of this study, we will collect questionnaire responses, laboratory data such as EEG, ECG and eye-tracking data, and information about your smartphone and social media use as described in the study information.

Your identifying information will be stored separately from your research data and used only where needed to manage your participation and link your study data using your participant ID.

text.text: I have previously provided informed consent to take part in this study, and I am happy to continue with the follow-up questionnaire and second laboratory session.
I understand that I am free to withdraw at any time without giving any reason and without there being any negative consequences

stem.text: Why your answers matter

lede.text:
There are no right or wrong answers here

What you tell us goes into research on how sleep, screens and feelings fit together for people your age, and on what actually helps. That only works if the answers are really yours, including the ones that aren't flattering.

A rushed or made-up answer doesn't just lose one number. It makes the whole picture slightly less true — for everyone the research is meant to help.

So take your time. And if you'd rather not answer something, leave it blank — that's always allowed.

items.researcherNote: Brief statement of why accurate responding matters, shown once after consent (D-30). Not a consent statement and carries no agreement — informational only.

The ps_id form was split into four single-purpose screens preceded by an explanation of what the code is for; birth month is now chosen from a list. Legacy ps_id is derived from ps_mother_initials + ps_house_digit + ps_birth_month + ps_postcode_letters at export, and val_id from the session's participant code — the crosswalk records both derivations rather than recoding silently. D-52: the secret code (its introduction and four components) is replaced by the home address, one form_fields screen with the postcode checked against the release's West Yorkshire list; the participant ID is derived from first name, last name and date of birth at ingest. D-53: someone who doesn't know their postcode can say so and find their street in a list of West Yorkshire's named roads.
ybm_identity@1.0/en-GB/self/standard.researcherNotes: Legacy crosswalk (r1.0.0–r7.3.0): ps_id = initials + house digit + zero-padded month number + postcode letters (e.g. JA101CD); val_id = the participant code captured at the opening screen. Both are derived, never re-asked. From r8.0.0 (D-52) there is no ps_id: the participant ID is P + ten base-32 characters of a hash of name and date of birth.

stem.text: Where would you be on this ladder?

lede.text:
Think of this ladder as representing where people stand in society in the UK.

At the top are the people who are best off — those who have the most money, the most education, and the most respected jobs.

At the bottom are the people who are worst off — those who have the least money, the least education, and the least respected jobs, or no job.

Where would you place yourself on this ladder at this time in your life?

score.swemwbs.provenance: SWEMWBS raw total (all 7 items required, per standard guidance). The metric-conversion lookup step is intentionally absent until the licensed conversion table is filed and transcribed (then added as version 1.1.0).

score.stai5.provenance: Zsido et al. (2020) STAI-5: sum of five 1-4 items. Verify no reverse-scored items against the publication before approval.

score.phq4.provenance: Kroenke et al. (2009): total 0–12 banded normal 0–2, mild 3–5, moderate 6–8, severe 9–12; GAD-2 and PHQ-2 each ≥3 suggests a positive screen.

score.bisbas12_ybm.provenance: Raw sums in administered coding (1=very true .. 4=very false); outputs suffixed _raw to signal direction is NOT yet normalised. Carver & White (1994) reverse-scoring convention for this subset to be verified before approval (A-22).
